C005.subject: Higher minimum wages
C005.object: employment in fast food in low-wage labor markets with high employer concentration when the wage increase is accompanied by a binding local labor supply constraint
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Higher minimum wages employment in fast food in low-wage labor markets with high employer concentration when the wage increase is accompanied by a binding local labor supply constraint]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data on local fast-food employment and minimum wage changes in U.S. metropolitan areas with high employer concentration (e.g., Herfindahl-Hirschman Index > 2500) from 2000-2020, combined with local labor supply tightness measures (e.g., low unemployment-to-vacancy ratios) — Directly tests the hypothesis by examining employment responses in precisely the scope conditions: concentrated markets with binding labor supply constraints, where theory predicts minimum wage increases could raise employment due to monopsony power.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of monopsonistic labor markets with wage floors and labor supply constraints (e.g., Bhaskar, Manning, & To, 2002; Manning, 2003) — Provides the formal framework to predict when a minimum wage increase can increase employment in concentrated markets with labor shortages, clarifying the necessary conditions and offering testable predictions for empirical work.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of minimum wage studies focused on fast-food employment in low-wage markets (e.g., Card & Krueger, 1994; Dube, Lester, & Reich, 2010; Allegretto et al., 2017), re-analyzed by sub-samples of high employer concentration and tight labor markets — Synthesizes existing empirical evidence to assess whether the hypothesized positive employment effect is consistently found under the specified conditions, or if it is an outlier result, thereby confirming or refuting the hypothesis.

scope.domain: low-wage, concentrated labor markets with labor shortages

qualifier.geographic: United States metropolitan areas with high employer concentration in fast food

C006.subject: Higher minimum wages
C006.object: employment in fast food in low-wage labor markets with high employer concentration
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Higher minimum wages employment in fast food in low-wage labor markets with high employer concentration]

[PATH:empirical] Card and Krueger (1994) minimum wage study reanalyzed with modern employer concentration data from the Census Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics (LEHD) program — Replicating the classic New Jersey-Pennsylvania fast-food study using current LEHD data on local employer concentration (e.g., Herfindahl-Hirschman Index) can directly test whether high concentration amplifies employment effects of minimum wage increases.

[PATH:empirical] Azar, Marinescu, and Steinbaum (2022) on labor market concentration and wages, extended to fast-food payroll data from the Quarterly Workforce Indicators (QWI) — This research direction uses QWI to measure employer concentration at the commuting zone level for fast-food workers, then tests interactions with minimum wage changes to see if employment rises more in highly concentrated low-wage markets.

[PATH:theoretical] Monopsony theory and simulation models (e.g., Manning, 2003) calibrated to fast-food industry parameters — Developing a search-and-matching model with employer market power and minimum wage floors can predict conditions under which employment increases, providing a theoretical benchmark to compare against empirical findings in concentrated labor markets.

[PATH:empirical] County-level panel data on fast-food employment and minimum wage changes, merged with local unemployment rates and worker-to-job ratios from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (LAUS and QCEW). — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing employment responses to minimum wage increases across counties with high vs. low worker-to-job ratios, controlling for turnover and demand spillovers.

[PATH:theoretical] A theoretical model of monopsonistic competition with heterogeneous labor market tightness, calibrated to fast-food industry parameters (e.g., Bhaskar, Manning, & To, 2002 or recent extensions). — Provides a causal mechanism explaining why slack labor markets amplify positive employment effects, and generates testable predictions about the role of outside options.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review or meta-analysis of minimum wage studies in service industries, focusing on effect heterogeneity by local labor market conditions (e.g., Dube, Lester, & Reich, 2010; Allegretto et al., 2017). — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the predicted pattern holds across multiple studies and identifies gaps in the current literature regarding worker-to-job ratios.

[PATH:empirical] Survey or case studies of fast-food franchise owners on hiring and automation decisions in response to minimum wage hikes (e.g., from National Restaurant Association or academic business surveys) — Provides micro-level evidence on the mechanism: whether increased labor costs lead to reduced hiring or accelerated adoption of automation (e.g., self-service kiosks).

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of labor demand and automation in low-skill service sectors (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo (2018) on automation and labor markets) — Offers a framework to predict under what conditions minimum wage increases cause employment declines via automation, helping interpret empirical results and scope conditions.
